title: Add Gateway API (HTTPRoute) support to Console Helm chart and CRD
body:
## Summary

Adds support for Kubernetes [Gateway API](https://gateway-api.sigs.k8s.io/) `HTTPRoute` resources to the Console chart and operator, allowing users to expose Console via Gateway API controllers (e.g. Envoy Gateway, Istio, Cilium) as an alternative to classic Ingress.

Closes #1308
Supersedes #1309 (recreated from upstream branch for CI)

Original chart work by @w1ndhunter.

## Prerequisites

Gateway API CRDs must be installed in your cluster before enabling this feature. The CRDs are **not** bundled with the Redpanda Helm chart or operator — they are maintained by the Kubernetes Gateway API project.

### Install Gateway API CRDs

```bash
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.5.1/standard-install.yaml
```

### Install a Gateway controller

You also need a Gateway API-compatible controller running in your cluster. Common options include:

- [Envoy Gateway](https://gateway.envoyproxy.io/)
- [Istio](https://istio.io/latest/docs/tasks/traffic-management/ingress/gateway-api/)
- [Cilium](https://docs.cilium.io/en/stable/network/servicemesh/gateway-api/gateway-api/)
- [NGINX Gateway Fabric](https://github.com/nginx/nginx-gateway-fabric)

Create a `Gateway` resource that the `HTTPRoute` will attach to:

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: my-gateway
  namespace: gateway-system
spec:
  gatewayClassName: eg  # varies by controller
  listeners:
    - name: https
      protocol: HTTPS
      port: 443
      tls:
        mode: Terminate
        certificateRefs:
          - name: my-tls-cert
```

## Changes

### Console Helm Chart
- New `gateway` values block alongside existing `ingress` block
- New `gateway.go` with `HTTPRoute()` rendering function
- `HTTPRoute` added to `Render()` manifest list and `Types()` scheme registration
- `gatewayv1.Install(Scheme)` for Gateway API type serialization
- Updated `notes.go` to show Gateway URLs (mutually exclusive with Ingress)
- Validation in `NewRenderState` rejects both gateway and ingress enabled simultaneously
- New test cases: gateway-only, mutual exclusion validation, gateway removal/switch scenarios
- Regenerated schema, golden files, and templates

### Operator (Console CRD)
- New `GatewayConfig` and `GatewayParentReference` types in `console_types.go`
- `Gateway` field added to `ConsoleValues` and `RedpandaConsole` structs
- Auto-generated conversion (goverter) from CRD types → chart partial values
- RBAC: added `gateway.networking.k8s.io/httproutes` permissions
- Registered `gatewayv1` types in V2 scheme
- Bumped `sigs.k8s.io/gateway-api` from v1.4.1 → v1.5.1
- Regenerated deepcopy, conversion, and CRD manifests
- HTTPRoute watch is skipped gracefully when Gateway API CRDs are not installed

### Console Controller Tests — Gateway API CRD Loading ⚠️

> **Reviewer note:** The console controller test (`operator/internal/controller/console/controller_test.go`) now loads Gateway API CRDs from the `sigs.k8s.io/gateway-api` Go module cache at test time. This is needed because envtest must have the HTTPRoute CRD installed for the controller to reconcile gateway-enabled Console objects (list HTTPRoutes, create/delete them).
>
> The `loadGatewayAPICRDs` helper resolves the module directory via `go list -m -f {{.Dir}} sigs.k8s.io/gateway-api`, reads all standard CRD YAMLs from `config/crd/standard/`, and parses them. Non-CRD files (e.g. `ValidatingAdmissionPolicy`) are skipped gracefully.
>
> This approach avoids vendoring the ~7K-line HTTPRoute CRD YAML into testdata while keeping the CRD version in sync with `go.mod`.

### Bug Fix: InUseServerCerts external TLS cert mounting
- Fixed `InUseServerCerts` in `charts/redpanda/values.go` (and `operator/multicluster/values.go`) where a `continue` statement on the internal listener's TLS check would skip registering external sub-listener certs. External certs are now checked independently of internal TLS state.

## Usage Examples

### Helm Chart — Gateway API

```bash
# 1. Install Gateway API CRDs (if not already installed)
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.5.1/standard-install.yaml

# 2. Install Console with gateway enabled
helm install console redpanda/console -f values.yaml
```

```yaml
# values.yaml
gateway:
  enabled: true
  annotations:
    example.com/owner: my-team
  parentRefs:
    - name: my-gateway
      namespace: gateway-system
      sectionName: https
  hostnames:
    - console.example.com
  path: /
  pathType: PathPrefix
```

### Helm Chart — Classic Ingress (unchanged)

```yaml
# values.yaml
ingress:
  enabled: true
  hosts:
    - host: console.example.com
      paths:
        - path: /
          pathType: Prefix
```

> **Note:** Enabling both `ingress.enabled: true` and `gateway.enabled: true` will fail with: `ingress and gateway cannot both be enabled; use one or the other`

### Console CRD (Operator) — Gateway API

```bash
# 1. Install Gateway API CRDs (if not already installed)
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.5.1/standard-install.yaml

# 2. Apply the Console CR with gateway enabled
kubectl apply -f console.yaml
```

```yaml
# console.yaml
apiVersion: cluster.redpanda.com/v1alpha2
kind: Console
metadata:
  name: my-console
  namespace: redpanda
spec:
  clusterSource:
    clusterRef:
      name: my-cluster
  gateway:
    enabled: true
    annotations:
      example.com/owner: my-team
    parentRefs:
      - name: my-gateway
        namespace: gateway-system
        sectionName: https
    hostnames:
      - console.example.com
    path: /
    pathType: PathPrefix
```

### Console CRD (Operator) — Switching from Gateway to Ingress

To switch, remove the `gateway` stanza and add `ingress`:

```yaml
apiVersion: cluster.redpanda.com/v1alpha2
kind: Console
metadata:
  name: my-console
  namespace: redpanda
spec:
  clusterSource:
    clusterRef:
      name: my-cluster
  ingress:
    enabled: true
    hosts:
      - host: console.example.com
        paths:
          - path: /
            pathType: Prefix
```

The operator will remove the HTTPRoute and create an Ingress instead.

## Test plan

- [ ] `go build ./...` passes in `operator/` and `charts/console/`
- [ ] `go test ./...` passes in `charts/console/` — includes:
  - `TestIngressGatewayMutualExclusion` — both enabled → error
  - `TestGatewayRemoval/gateway_removed_from_config` — no gateway stanza → no HTTPRoute
  - `TestGatewayRemoval/gateway_explicitly_disabled` — `enabled: false` → no HTTPRoute
  - `TestGatewayRemoval/switch_from_gateway_to_ingress` — gateway→ingress produces Ingress, no HTTPRoute
  - `TestTemplate` golden tests (gateway-templating case)
- [ ] Console controller tests pass with Gateway API CRDs loaded into envtest
  - `TestController/gateway-enabled` — basic gateway with parentRefs
  - `TestController/gateway-custom-path` — custom path and multiple parentRefs
- [ ] CRD schema includes `gateway` field with correct OpenAPI validation
- [ ] Deploy Console CRD with `gateway.enabled: true` → HTTPRoute created
- [ ] Deploy via Helm with `gateway.enabled: true` → HTTPRoute created
- [ ] Enabling both ingress and gateway → validation error

title: operator: adopt per-broker pre-restart probe (ENG-222) + roll-loop correctness
body:
## Summary

Adopt Redpanda 25.1+'s per-broker pre-restart probe (ENG-222) as the primary
rolling-restart gate, replacing the cluster-wide `health_overview.IsHealthy`
heuristic with the per-broker counterfactual `/v1/broker/pre_restart_probe`.

This PR is the consolidated customer-blocking fix for the rolling-restart
races; it folds in the two correctness fixes from the (now-closed) #1537 so
they don't get lost.

## Failure modes this prevents

Each item below is a concrete cluster-level failure a rolling restart could
cause *before* this PR, and the gate that now prevents it. Items 1–2 are
literal multi-broker-down bugs; items 3–4 are timing races where the cluster
looks healthy but a restart is still unsafe.

1. **Multiple brokers `Terminating` simultaneously → lost Raft quorum / cluster
   unavailable.** The `!inBrokerMap` branch deleted *every* unmapped pod in a
   single reconcile pass. Combined with item 2 — or any transient cause that
   empties `health.AllNodes` (controller-leadership change, a brief admin-API
   `503`, a NodeID flip after a PVC reset) — the whole `rollSet` could be torn
   down at once, dropping two or more brokers together and taking the cluster
   (and its controller quorum) offline. **Now:** one pod is deleted per
   reconcile, then the controller requeues and re-evaluates against a fresh
   broker view before touching the next pod — and an unmapped pod is deleted
   *only while `health.IsHealthy`*, since it has no broker ID to pre-restart-probe
   and may actually be a live in-sync replica.

2. **A live, in-sync broker mis-classified as an orphan and deleted.**
   `strings.Split(InternalRPCAddress, ".")[0]` produced the wrong map key when
   the admin API returned the address as `host:port` (advertised RPC port
   suffix) or as a bare IP. `brokerMap[pod.GetName()]` then missed, and the
   roll loop treated a healthy broker as an orphan and deleted it. **Now:** the
   port is stripped with `net.SplitHostPort` and each broker is keyed by both
   its first DNS label and its raw host, so the lookup matches.

3. **Restarting a broker that the cluster-wide health check wrongly thinks is
   safe → acks=1 data loss, acks=-1 produce rejection, or leaderless
   partitions.** `health.IsHealthy` is a single cluster-wide boolean; it can
   read `true` while restarting one *specific* broker would still (a) lose
   acks=1-acknowledged data, (b) leave no quorum for acks=-1 produce, or (c)
   make partitions leaderless. **Now:** the per-broker pre-restart probe
   (`/v1/broker/pre_restart_probe`) answers the counterfactual "if I restart
   *this* broker now, what breaks?" and blocks the roll when any of
   `acks1_data_loss`, `unavailable`, or `full_acks_produce_unavailable` is
   populated. `rf1_offline` is treated as acceptable (RF=1 already has no
   redundancy).

4. **Rolling the next broker before the previous one finished recovering →
   under-replication / stalled produce.** K8s pod-Ready (the existing
   `HasRecentlyReplacedPods` gate) can flip `true` while the broker inside is
   still replaying partition state from its peers. Rolling the next broker in
   that window removes a second replica before the first is back in-sync; with
   RF=3 a two-down window can stall acks=all produce. **Now:** the post-restart
   probe (`/v1/broker/post_restart_probe`, `load_reclaimed_pc >= 100`) holds
   the next roll until the recovering broker reports it has caught up. The
   per-broker scan keeps going after a probe error, so a confirmed
   still-recovering broker is never masked by an unrelated error (the caller
   otherwise treats probe errors as non-fatal and would proceed).

Net effect: rolling restarts under load no longer hit the customer-visible
"1 broker `Terminating` + 1 broker `NotReady`" window, nor the
`IsHealthy == true` while a broker is still partition-recovering race. On
Redpanda < 25.1 (probe endpoints return `404`) behavior is unchanged — the
helpers fall back to the prior `health.IsHealthy` path, and the K8s-Ready and
one-pod-per-reconcile gates still apply.

## How the pre/post-restart probes are used (core ↔ operator) and firing order

**What Redpanda core provides** (25.1+, per-broker — the probe answers for the
broker that handles the request, so the operator scopes the client to one broker
via `BrokerIDToURL` + `ForHost`):

- `GET /v1/broker/pre_restart_probe` → `{"risks": {"acks1_data_loss": [...],
  "unavailable": [...], "full_acks_produce_unavailable": [...], "rf1_offline": [...]}}`
  — the counterfactual *"if this broker is restarted right now, which partitions are at risk?"*
- `GET /v1/broker/post_restart_probe` → `{"load_reclaimed_pc": N}` — how much of its
  in-sync-replica load the broker has reclaimed since its last restart (0–100; 100 = caught up).

**How the operator interprets them** (`internal/probes/broker.go`):

- `brokerSafeToRestart` (**pre**): safe iff `acks1_data_loss` + `unavailable` +
  `full_acks_produce_unavailable` are all empty (`rf1_offline` is acceptable — RF=1
  already has no redundancy). On 404 (pre-25.1) → fall back to cluster `IsHealthy`.
- `brokersStillRecovering` / `brokerCaughtUp` (**post**): caught up ⟺
  `load_reclaimed_pc >= 100`. On 404 → treat as caught up.

**Evaluation order within one `reconcileDecommission` pass** (over `PodsToRoll()`):

1. `HasRecentlyReplacedPods()` — K8s pod-Ready gate (#1446): if a just-replaced pod
   isn't Ready, requeue.
2. `brokersStillRecovering(...)` — **POST-restart probe**, an *outer* gate across
   **all** brokers: if any reports `load_reclaimed_pc < 100`, requeue (roll no one).
3. per-pod loop → `brokerSafeToRestart(...)` — **PRE-restart probe** for the specific
   candidate broker: if it reports a dangerous risk, skip it; if safe, delete the pod
   (roll it) and requeue.

**Per-broker lifecycle across a rolling restart** (one broker per reconcile, then
requeue — maps to the ENG-222 RFC's 6-step ideal sequence):

```
for each broker Bi:
  (RFC 1) maintenance mode ON     ← chart preStop hook on pod delete (not the operator)
  (RFC 2) PRE-restart probe(Bi)   ← brokerSafeToRestart, BEFORE deleting the pod
          delete pod (roll Bi)
  (RFC 3) wait broker available   ← HasRecentlyReplacedPods (K8s-Ready) on later reconciles
  (RFC 4) maintenance mode OFF    ← chart postStart hook
  (RFC 5) POST-restart probe(Bi)  ← brokersStillRecovering holds until load_reclaimed_pc=100
  (RFC 6) proceed to Bi+1
```

In short: for a given broker the **pre-restart probe fires before its roll**, and its
**post-restart probe gates the *next* broker's roll** — the operator won't
pre-restart-probe/roll `Bi+1` until `Bi` is both K8s-Ready *and* `load_reclaimed_pc=100`.
Maintenance-mode drain (RFC steps 1/4) is the chart's preStop/postStart hooks, triggered
by the operator's pod delete — not the operator itself.

**Performance impact.** Both probe gates are behind `if len(rollSet) > 0`, so they fire
**only during an active rolling restart** — steady-state reconciliation makes **no** probe
calls. (The per-reconcile `brokerMap` build is pre-existing and unchanged.) While a roll is
in progress, the added cost per reconcile is one `post_restart_probe` GET per broker
(deduped) plus one `pre_restart_probe` GET per candidate pod — lightweight admin-API calls
on the ~10s requeue cadence for the bounded duration of the roll. The server-side probe work
is bounded (the `limit` query param caps it at 128 partitions per risk category), and the
pre-25.1 404 path is a cheap round-trip. The deferrals the post-restart gate introduces are
*intentional* safety waits (holding the next roll until a broker re-syncs), not wasted work.
Measured on the 6-broker / 60-partition / high-throughput E2E: no material impact — the PR
arm completed **8 rolls vs main's 7** in the same window with comparable acks=1 throughput
(1.39M vs 1.36M acked) and no producer-throughput degradation. (Minor: `admin.ForHost` builds
a fresh scoped client per probe call; negligible at realistic fleet sizes during a roll, a
candidate for client reuse only if probing very large clusters.)

## Why all together

The changes cover four independent failure surfaces that all contribute to
the same customer-visible bug:

| Concern | What's broken | What this PR does |
|---|---|---|
| Multiple deletes per reconcile | `!inBrokerMap` branch tear-down | one-pod-per-reconcile |
| Address-format misclassification | `strings.Split(...)[0]` parser | `net.SplitHostPort` + dual-key |
| Coarse-grained roll signal | `health.IsHealthy` (cluster-wide) | per-broker `PreRestartProbe` |
| K8s pod-Ready ≠ broker caught up | new broker passes pod-Ready before it has finished replaying partition state | per-broker `PostRestartProbe` outer gate |

Together they make rolling restart safe under load, both for the literal
parallel-delete scenario (the orphan-branch fix) and the timing race where
the cluster reports `IsHealthy=true` while a broker is still partition-
recovering (the pre- and post-restart probes).

## Dependencies

- `github.com/redpanda-data/common-go/rpadmin v0.2.7` (carries
  `PreRestartProbe`/`PostRestartProbe` from common-go#170)
- `github.com/testcontainers/testcontainers-go v0.42.0` (already present)
- Cleanup: dropped `github.com/moby/moby/pkg/namesgenerator` (single-line use
  in `cluster_controller_configuration_test.go`) because the moby monolith
  v28+ conflicts with the split-out `moby/moby/api` module pulled in via
  testcontainers v0.42's transitive deps under rpadmin v0.2.7. Replaced with
  a 4-byte `crypto/rand` hex suffix.

## Tests

`TestIntegrationBrokerSafeToRestart` boots a real Redpanda container via
testcontainers (for the live-probe subtests) and uses httptest stubs
(for the RFC-case and error-handling subtests). Twelve subtests pin the
pre-restart contract:

| Subtest | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `fresh cluster is safe to restart` | A broker with no partitions reports safe (live broker) |
| `RF=1 topic still counts as safe (acceptable risk)` | rf1_offline is populated but the helper still returns safe (live broker) |
| `404 falls back to cluster.IsHealthy` | Pre-25.1 broker → returns the cluster-health argument unchanged (both true and false directions pinned) |
| `non-404 admin errors surface as errors` | 5xx propagates instead of silently falling back |
| **RFC case 1**: in-sync 2, offline 1 — restarting online replica makes partition leaderless | blocks on `unavailable` |
| **RFC case 2 (in-sync restart)**: in-sync 2, recovering 1 — restarting in-sync replica blocks acks=-1 produce | blocks on `full_acks_produce_unavailable` |
| **RFC case 2 (recovering-replica restart)** | empty risks → safe to restart |
| **RFC case 3**: in-sync 1, offline 1, recovering 1 — restarting in-sync risks acks=1 data loss | blocks even when both `unavailable` and `acks1_data_loss` are populated |
| **RFC case 4**: in-sync 1, recovering 2 — restarting in-sync causes acks=1 data loss | blocks on `acks1_data_loss` |
| RF=1 acceptable + dangerous category populated | still blocked — rf1 doesn't override |
| all categories empty | safe (steady-state happy path) |

The RFC cases reference the rolling-restart safety probes RFC's
"Scenarios" section. Reproducing the actual multi-broker cluster states
inside a single testcontainer isn't practical; Redpanda core's own
suite verifies server-side risk calculation per cluster state. What
this test pins is the operator's *interpretation* of the wire
contract — for each documented failure mode, the JSON the probe
returns translates to the right roll decision.

Verified locally against `redpandadata/redpanda:v26.1.1`:

```
PASS  TestIntegrationBrokerSafeToRestart (19.042s) — 12/12 subtests
```

`TestIntegrationBrokerCaughtUp` + `TestIntegrationBrokersStillRecovering`
pin the post-restart contract (10 subtests total) via httptest stubs:

| Subtest | What it pins |
|---|---|
| `fully caught up at default threshold` | 100% → caught up |
| `99% not caught up at default strict threshold` | strict default blocks |
| `99% caught up at relaxed threshold (95)` | threshold is honored |
| `0% (just restarted) not caught up` | freshly-restarted broker blocks |
| `404 falls back to caught up (pre-25.1 broker)` | older Redpanda → not blocked |
| `500 propagates as error` | admin failure surfaces |
| `any broker below threshold blocks` | gate fires if *any* broker is recovering |
| `all brokers caught up returns false` | clean steady state |
| `dedupes by broker ID across map entries` | brokerMap's double-key doesn't double-probe |
| `404 on a broker is treated as endpoint absent` | mixed-version cluster behaves safely |

```
PASS  TestIntegrationBrokerCaughtUp (3.03s)              — 6/6
PASS  TestIntegrationBrokersStillRecovering (0.00s)      — 4/4
```

`TestHasRecentlyReplacedPods` in `internal/lifecycle/pool_test.go` — 6 cases,
all pass locally.

Run with:

```bash
DOCKER_HOST=unix:///path/to/docker.sock \
TESTCONTAINERS_DOCKER_SOCKET_OVERRIDE=/var/run/docker.sock \
TESTCONTAINERS_RYUK_DISABLED=true \
GOLANG_PROTOBUF_REGISTRATION_CONFLICT=ignore \
TEST_REDPANDA_REPO=redpandadata/redpanda TEST_REDPANDA_VERSION=v26.1.1 \
nix develop -c go test ./operator/internal/controller/redpanda/ \
  -run TestIntegrationBrokerSafeToRestart -v -count=1 -timeout 360s
```

## Test plan

- [x] `go build ./operator/internal/probes/... ./operator/internal/controller/redpanda/... ./operator/internal/lifecycle/...` — clean
- [x] `go vet` on the same — clean
- [x] `TestIntegrationBrokerSafeToRestart` against real `v26.1.1` — green
- [x] `TestIntegrationBrokerCaughtUp` / `TestIntegrationBrokersStillRecovering` (incl. the post-restart probe-error regression) — green
- [x] `TestHasRecentlyReplacedPods` — green
- [x] `gofmt` — clean
- [x] Full unit suite — green (CI build #14362: Unit Tests)
- [x] Acceptance suite (incl. under-load rolling-restart) — green (CI build #14362:
      Acceptance + Acceptance-Multicluster + Kuttl-Nodepools)
- [x] EKS E2E (6-broker, high-throughput, sustained rolls): probes fire at scale
      (88 post-restart deferrals + 32 pre-restart blocks vs main 0/0), 0 acks=1
      loss, one-pod-per-reconcile holds — see `redpanda-setup/operator-health-probe/`

## Follow-ups (not in this PR)

- **Opt-in acks=1 tolerance.** The RFC explicitly punts: *"For the
  acks=1 case... we should prioritize making forward progress in the
  rolling restart process as well, though automatically determining if
  possible data loss is 'legitimate'... may prove hard."* Current
  default is strict (always block on `acks1_data_loss`). A CR-level
  knob could allow opt-in tolerance for clusters that have explicitly
  accepted the trade-off. Separate PR.
- **PreRestartProbe equivalent for stretch / multicluster controller.** This
  PR wires only the single-cluster controller. The multicluster controller
  (which we'll be removing) is unchanged.
- **Chart-side preStop drain hardening.** #1548 (merged) surfaced drain
  timeouts in pod logs but deliberately kept the `; true` fail-open behavior,
  so the maintenance-mode drain is still best-effort. A future option could
  make the drain block termination (or extend its budget under load) for
  fully graceful handoff; not required for the data-loss guarantee, which is
  enforced by the pre-restart probe in this PR.

title: operator: support cross-namespace clusterRef for shadow links (K8S-816)
body:
## What

Resolves [K8S-816](https://redpandadata.atlassian.net/browse/K8S-816): support a `ShadowLink` (and other `clusterRef`-based resources) referencing a Redpanda cluster in a **different namespace** on the **same** Kubernetes cluster.

Previously every `clusterRef` was resolved in the referencing object's own namespace (`obj.GetNamespace()` was hardcoded in the client factory and the field indexer), so a `ShadowLink` in namespace `b` could not point its `sourceCluster.clusterRef` at a Redpanda cluster in namespace `a`.

> **Recommended for test & dev clusters.** Running the source and shadow clusters in
> two namespaces on a **single** Kubernetes cluster is intended primarily to rehearse
> shadow-link replication and failover cheaply (one cluster, no second region). For
> AZ-level fault isolation in dev/test, pin the two clusters to **non-overlapping
> availability zones** (see "Test/dev topology" below). **Production disaster recovery**
> should still use **separate clusters in separate failure domains/regions.**

## Changes

- **`ClusterRef.Namespace`** — new optional field. When unset, resolution falls back to the referencing object's namespace (fully backwards compatible). Added a `GetNamespace(fallback)` helper.
- **Factory resolvers** (`operator/pkg/client/factory.go`) — all five cluster lookups (`getV1Cluster`, `getRemoteV1Cluster`, `getV2Cluster`, `getRemoteV2Cluster`, `getStretchCluster`) now honor the ref namespace.
- **Field index** (`operator/internal/controller/index.go`) — `indexByClusterSource` now keys on the ref namespace so a change to a cross-namespace source cluster enqueues the referencing object. Also fixes a latent bug where the remote-source branch checked `source.ClusterRef` instead of `remoteSource.ClusterRef`.
- Regenerated CRDs, deepcopy, applyconfiguration, and CRD docs. The field is shared, so it appears on all `clusterRef` consumers (`ShadowLink`, `Topic`, `User`, `Role`, `Schema`, `Group`).

Connectivity needs no change: bootstrap servers are internal `*.svc.cluster.local` addresses that already resolve cluster-wide; only the CR lookup needed to honor the namespace.

## Usage: shadow link across namespaces

Two Redpanda clusters on the **same** Kubernetes cluster, in separate namespaces (`a` = source, `b` = shadow). Both must have `enable_shadow_linking: true`.

```yaml
# Source cluster in namespace "a"
apiVersion: cluster.redpanda.com/v1alpha2
kind: Redpanda
metadata: { name: redpanda-source, namespace: a }
spec:
  clusterSpec:
    config: { cluster: { enable_shadow_linking: true, default_topic_replications: 1 } }
---
# Shadow cluster in namespace "b"
apiVersion: cluster.redpanda.com/v1alpha2
kind: Redpanda
metadata: { name: redpanda-target, namespace: b }
spec:
  clusterSpec:
    config: { cluster: { enable_shadow_linking: true, default_topic_replications: 1 } }
```

The `ShadowLink` lives alongside the shadow cluster in namespace `b`. The **new `namespace` field** on `sourceCluster.clusterRef` is what makes the cross-namespace reference possible — without it the operator would look for `redpanda-source` in namespace `b` and fail with `ClusterRefInvalid`:

```yaml
apiVersion: cluster.redpanda.com/v1alpha2
kind: ShadowLink
metadata:
  name: disaster-recovery-link
  namespace: b
spec:
  shadowCluster:
    clusterRef:
      name: redpanda-target        # resolved in the ShadowLink's namespace (b)
  sourceCluster:
    clusterRef:
      name: redpanda-source
      namespace: a                 # <-- NEW: cross-namespace reference (this PR)
  topicMetadataSyncOptions:
    interval: 5s
    autoCreateShadowTopicFilters:
      - { name: '*', filterType: include, patternType: literal }
  consumerOffsetSyncOptions:
    interval: 5s
```

Verify the link is established:

```console
$ kubectl -n b get shadowlink disaster-recovery-link
NAME                     SYNCED
disaster-recovery-link   True
```

Topics produced on the source are auto-created as read-only shadow topics on the target and appear in `.status.shadowTopicStatuses` with `state: active`.

### Test/dev topology: both clusters on one EKS, non-overlapping AZs

For cheap DR rehearsal, run both clusters on one EKS cluster (this PR's cross-namespace
support) with AZ-level isolation. **`us-east-1` has 6 AZs**, so each cluster can run a full
**3-broker, 3-AZ** spread on **disjoint** zones — no AZ hosts brokers from both clusters:

- source (ns `a`) → `us-east-1a` / `us-east-1b` / `us-east-1c`
- shadow (ns `b`) → `us-east-1d` / `us-east-1e` / `us-east-1f`

```yaml
# Source (ns a) — brokers pinned to us-east-1a / 1b / 1c
spec:
  clusterSpec:
    statefulset:
      replicas: 3
      podTemplate:
        spec:
          affinity:
            nodeAffinity:
              requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
                nodeSelectorTerms:
                - matchExpressions:
                  - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                    operator: In
                    values: ["us-east-1a", "us-east-1b", "us-east-1c"]
---
# Shadow (ns b) — brokers pinned to the DISJOINT us-east-1d / 1e / 1f
spec:
  clusterSpec:
    statefulset:
      replicas: 3
      podTemplate:
        spec:
          affinity:
            nodeAffinity:
              requiredDuringSchedulingIgnoredDuringExecution:
                nodeSelectorTerms:
                - matchExpressions:
                  - key: topology.kubernetes.io/zone
                    operator: In
                    values: ["us-east-1d", "us-east-1e", "us-east-1f"]
```

Give the EKS managed node group subnets in all six AZs (verify your account/instance types
support the chosen AZs — `us-east-1e` lacks some instance types). Each cluster then runs a
full 3-AZ HA spread in its own three zones, fully disjoint from the other — real AZ-level
fault isolation between source and shadow on a single cluster/region, ideal for dev/test.
Production DR should still use separate clusters/regions.

## Failover using CRDs

With today's operator the CRD-driven failover lever is **deleting the `ShadowLink`**. The operator calls `DeleteShadowLink(Force=true)`, which releases the shadow topics on the target and promotes them to normal **writable** topics, preserving all replicated data. A typical DR runbook:

```console
# 1. Source region/cluster is down. Confirm the target has the replicated data:
$ kubectl -n b exec redpanda-target-0 -c redpanda -- rpk topic describe events -p

# 2. Trigger failover by deleting the ShadowLink CR:
$ kubectl -n b delete shadowlink disaster-recovery-link

# 3. The shadow topics on the target are now writable. Point producers/consumers
#    at redpanda-target.b.svc.cluster.local:9093 and resume traffic.
```

Before failover, producing to a shadow topic on the target is rejected with `POLICY_VIOLATION` (read-only mirror). After deleting the `ShadowLink`, the same produce succeeds.

> Note: the Redpanda admin API also exposes a dedicated `FailOver` RPC (per-link or per-topic) that the operator does not yet surface as a CRD field. A first-class `spec.failover`/promotion field is a reasonable follow-up; this PR keeps scope to cross-namespace resolution and documents the delete-based path that works today.

## E2E validation (EKS 1.34)

Validated on a freshly provisioned **EKS 1.34** cluster (`v1.34.8-eks`, us-west-2, 3× m5.xlarge) with the operator image built from this branch:

1. Installed the operator (`crds.experimental=true`); confirmed the deployed `ShadowLink` CRD exposes the new `sourceCluster.clusterRef.namespace` field (`kubectl explain`).
2. Deployed `redpanda-source` (ns `a`) and `redpanda-target` (ns `b`), both `enable_shadow_linking: true`.
3. Applied the cross-namespace `ShadowLink` above → `SYNCED=True`, `state: active`.
4. Produced 200 records to `events` on the source → auto-created shadow topic on the target with all 200 records replicated (verified by consume + high-watermark); `shadowTopicStatuses[].state=active`.
5. **Failover:** scaled the source to 0 (outage), deleted the `ShadowLink` CR → target `events` flipped from read-only (`POLICY_VIOLATION`) to writable; produced 50 new records while retaining the 200 shadowed ones (250 total).
6. **Under load:** OMB sustained **1.000 MB/s** (1024 msg/s × 1 KB, p50 publish latency ~4.8 ms) against the
   source; the OMB topic auto-created as a shadow topic on the target and replicated cross-namespace in
   near-real-time (target high-watermark tracked the source while producing).
7. **Failover under load:** scaled the source to 0 (outage) — target shadow topic stayed read-only
   (`POLICY_VIOLATION`); deleting the `ShadowLink` CR promoted it to writable, retaining **~183.6k replicated
   records (zero loss)**, and a post-failover write succeeded.

Reproduction manifests, the OMB image Dockerfile, and a `run.sh` are kept under `redpanda-setup/shadow-cross-namespace`.

## Testing

- `go build` of `operator/api`, `operator/pkg/client`, `operator/internal/controller`
- New unit test `TestClusterRefGetNamespace`
- `task generate` + lint clean (golangci-lint, helm lint --strict, actionlint)

title: charts/redpanda: Gateway API TLSRoute support for external Kafka access (per-listener type)
body:
## Summary

- Adds Gateway API TLSRoute-based external access as an alternative to NodePort/LoadBalancer
- Per-listener `type: tlsroute` enables gradual migration — traditional and TLSRoute listeners coexist
- Creates bootstrap and per-broker ClusterIP services as TLSRoute backends
- Per-listener `host`/`hostTemplate` fields enable unique SNI hostnames per external listener, solving the per-listener domain problem (#1361)
- User manages the Gateway externally; the chart only creates TLSRoute resources referencing it via `parentRefs`
- Reports Gateway API external-access adoption through operator telemetry (`gatewayAPIExternalAccessEnabled`)

## Design

The design follows the established pattern for TLSRoute-based access using Gateway API:

1. **User brings their own Gateway** — the operator/chart only manages TLSRoute resources and ClusterIP services
2. **Per-listener opt-in** — each external listener independently selects gateway mode via `type: tlsroute` (overriding the cluster-wide `external.type`), enabling gradual migration
3. **SNI-based routing** — each broker gets a unique hostname, allowing the Gateway to route TLS traffic by SNI to the correct per-broker service
4. **Bootstrap + per-broker architecture** — a bootstrap TLSRoute handles initial client connections; per-broker TLSRoutes handle direct broker connections after metadata discovery

## External access model: per-listener `type` (alias layer)

External access type is set cluster-wide via `external.type` (`NodePort` or `LoadBalancer`). Each external listener may override it with its own `type`, which acts as a thin alias layer on top of the cluster default:

- **unset (default)** — the listener inherits `external.type` (conventional NodePort/LoadBalancer). Existing configurations are unchanged.
- **`type: tlsroute`** — the listener is routed via Gateway API: a bootstrap + per-broker TLSRoute is created and the listener is **excluded** from the NodePort/LoadBalancer Service.

The per-listener `type` is **authoritative**: a `tlsroute` listener is never placed in a conventional Service regardless of global state, and render **fails closed** if `type: tlsroute` is set without `external.gateway` configured (`enabled` + at least one `parentRef`). This makes the gateway-vs-conventional decision unambiguous per listener and is what enables gradual migration — a conventional listener and a `tlsroute` listener can coexist on different ports during cutover. (There is no separate `gateway: true` flag; the listener `type` is the single opt-in, leaving room to grow the enum toward fully per-listener external types later.)

## Why `hostTemplate` and not the existing `prefixTemplate`

The chart already has a per-listener `prefixTemplate` for external advertised addresses, so why add a new `host`/`hostTemplate` pair? Two reasons specific to Gateway API SNI routing:

1. **Per-listener full hostnames / per-listener domains (#1361).** `prefixTemplate` templates only the *prefix*; the suffix is the single global `external.domain`. SNI routing needs each external listener to resolve to its own full hostname, and #1361 specifically asks for *different domains per listener* — which a global-domain `prefixTemplate` cannot express. `host`/`hostTemplate` are full hostnames, set independently per listener.

2. **Render-time vs runtime evaluation.** A `TLSRoute` is a static resource whose SNI hostnames must be known at **chart-render time**. `prefixTemplate` is evaluated at **runtime inside the configurator initContainer**, where it may use values the chart cannot predict (`$HOST_IP_ADDRESS`, arbitrary shell `$(...)`); those cannot drive a static TLSRoute SNI. `hostTemplate` is deliberately restricted to render-time substitutions (`$POD_ORDINAL`, `$POD_NAME`), so the rendered TLSRoute SNI and the broker's advertised address are produced by the **same** `renderBrokerHost()` and are guaranteed to match — the broker advertises exactly the hostname the Gateway routes by SNI.

So `hostTemplate` is not a duplicate of `prefixTemplate`: it solves the SNI / per-listener-domain problem that `prefixTemplate` structurally cannot. `prefixTemplate` continues to govern the traditional NodePort/LoadBalancer advertised-address path, unchanged.

## Gateway API version compatibility

TLSRoute is **GA** (`gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1`) as of Gateway API v1.5, and this PR renders and watches the GA `v1` type (`sigs.k8s.io/gateway-api` pinned to v1.5.1). Because `v1` is a GA API with the project's backward-compatibility guarantees, **the gateway-api dependency does not need to be bumped on every Gateway API release to stay compatible**:

- The operator renders a stable `v1` TLSRoute that is accepted by any cluster carrying the `v1` TLSRoute CRD (Gateway API **≥ v1.5**) and a TLSRoute-capable Gateway implementation. Compatibility is determined by the CRD version present in the cluster, not by the operator's lib version.
- Bumping `sigs.k8s.io/gateway-api` is only needed to *adopt new optional fields* introduced in a later release — not to maintain compatibility.
- This is a direct benefit of moving off the experimental `v1alpha2` API. While TLSRoute was experimental, alpha versions churned (e.g. Gateway API v1.4 made `v1alpha3` the storage version), which forced the operator and the Gateway implementation to track each other closely. GA `v1` ends that churn.

**Cluster requirements:** Gateway API **≥ v1.5** (experimental channel — TLSRoute ships there) and a Gateway implementation that supports TLSRoute `v1` (e.g. Envoy Gateway ≥ v1.8). Validated end-to-end on EKS 1.36 + Gateway API v1.5.1 + Envoy Gateway v1.8.1 (operator-managed `Redpanda` CR, produce + consume over TLS through the Gateway).

> **Envoy Gateway note:** its Helm chart does not ship a default `GatewayClass`, so you must create one (e.g. `kubectl apply` a `GatewayClass` named `eg` with `controllerName: gateway.envoyproxy.io/gatewayclass-controller`) before the Gateway in the examples below will be reconciled. The recipe in [Verified end-to-end with Envoy Gateway + `rpk`](#verified-end-to-end-with-envoy-gateway--rpk) includes this step.

## Using TLS Passthrough (recommended)

In passthrough mode, the Gateway forwards the TLS connection as-is to the Redpanda broker. Redpanda's own TLS certificate is used, and mTLS authentication works.

```
Client ──[TLS]──▶ Gateway ──[TLS passthrough]──▶ Redpanda broker
```

### Step 1: Create a Gateway with TLS passthrough

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: redpanda-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: envoy   # or any TLSRoute-capable implementation
  listeners:
    - name: kafka
      protocol: TLS
      port: 9094
      tls:
        mode: Passthrough    # forward TLS as-is to Redpanda
```

### Step 2: Configure Redpanda with gateway listeners

```yaml
external:
  enabled: true
  gateway:
    enabled: true
    parentRefs:
      - name: redpanda-gateway
        sectionName: kafka
    advertisedPort: 9094
tls:
  enabled: true
  certs:
    default:
      caEnabled: true
listeners:
  kafka:
    external:
      default:
        port: 9094
        type: tlsroute                                  # opt-in to TLSRoute mode
        host: redpanda.example.com                     # bootstrap hostname
        hostTemplate: redpanda-$POD_ORDINAL-broker.example.com  # per-broker hostname
        tls:
          enabled: true
          cert: default
```

### What the chart renders for this listener

With `helm install redpanda … --set statefulset.replicas=3`, the `default` listener above renders **one bootstrap TLSRoute + one TLSRoute per broker**, all attached to the `kafka` section of your Gateway via `parentRefs`. Each route's `hostnames` entry is the SNI the Gateway matches on (produced by the same `renderBrokerHost()` that builds the broker's advertised address, so they always match); `backendRefs` points at the chart-created ClusterIP service for that broker. Note the backend `port` is the **listener** port (`9094`); `advertisedPort` only governs what the broker advertises in metadata.

```yaml
# Bootstrap — initial client connections (host: redpanda.example.com)
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: TLSRoute
metadata:
  name: redpanda-kafka-default-bootstrap
  namespace: default
spec:
  hostnames:
  - redpanda.example.com
  parentRefs:
  - name: kafka-gateway
    sectionName: kafka
  rules:
  - backendRefs:
    - name: redpanda-gateway-bootstrap   # ClusterIP service load-balancing all brokers
      port: 9094
---
# Per-broker — direct connections after metadata discovery (hostTemplate, $POD_ORDINAL → 0)
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: TLSRoute
metadata:
  name: redpanda-kafka-default-0
  namespace: default
spec:
  hostnames:
  - redpanda-0-broker.example.com
  parentRefs:
  - name: kafka-gateway
    sectionName: kafka
  rules:
  - backendRefs:
    - name: gw-redpanda-0                 # ClusterIP service selecting pod redpanda-0
      port: 9094
---
# redpanda-kafka-default-1 → redpanda-1-broker.example.com → gw-redpanda-1:9094
# redpanda-kafka-default-2 → redpanda-2-broker.example.com → gw-redpanda-2:9094
#   (identical shape; one route per replica)
```

Naming pattern: TLSRoute `‹release›-‹listener-protocol›-‹listener-name›-{bootstrap|‹ordinal›}`, bootstrap service `‹release›-gateway-bootstrap`, per-broker service `gw-‹release›-‹ordinal›`. NodePort/LoadBalancer services are **not** rendered for a gateway-opted listener.

### Step 3: Configure DNS

Point these DNS records to the Gateway's external IP:
- `redpanda.example.com` → Gateway IP (bootstrap)
- `redpanda-0-broker.example.com` → Gateway IP (broker 0)
- `redpanda-1-broker.example.com` → Gateway IP (broker 1)
- `redpanda-2-broker.example.com` → Gateway IP (broker 2)

### Step 4: Connect clients

```bash
rpk topic list \
  --brokers redpanda.example.com:9094 \
  --tls-enabled \
  --tls-truststore ca.crt
```

## Using TLS Termination

In termination mode, the Gateway decrypts TLS and forwards plaintext to the broker. The Gateway's own certificate is presented to clients. mTLS authentication is **not available** in this mode.

> **Note**: TLS termination for TLSRoutes is not yet supported by most Gateway implementations. Passthrough is the practical choice today.

```
Client ──[TLS]──▶ Gateway ──[plaintext]──▶ Redpanda broker
```

### Step 1: Create a Gateway with TLS termination

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: redpanda-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: envoy
  listeners:
    - name: kafka
      protocol: TLS
      port: 9094
      tls:
        mode: Terminate       # Gateway decrypts TLS
        certificateRefs:
          - name: gateway-tls-cert
```

### Step 2: Configure Redpanda without TLS on the external listener

Since the Gateway handles TLS, the Redpanda listener receives plaintext:

```yaml
external:
  enabled: true
  gateway:
    enabled: true
    parentRefs:
      - name: redpanda-gateway
        sectionName: kafka
    advertisedPort: 9094
listeners:
  kafka:
    external:
      default:
        port: 9094
        type: tlsroute
        host: redpanda.example.com
        hostTemplate: redpanda-$POD_ORDINAL-broker.example.com
        # No TLS config — connection arrives decrypted from the Gateway
```

### What the chart renders for this listener

The rendered TLSRoutes are **identical to the passthrough example above** (`redpanda-kafka-default-bootstrap` + `redpanda-kafka-default-0…2`, backend port `9094`). A TLSRoute only describes SNI-based routing to a backend service — it carries no TLS material — so it is unaffected by whether the listener itself enables TLS. The passthrough-vs-terminate distinction lives entirely in the **Gateway** listener's `tls.mode`, not in what the chart renders.

## Migrating from Traditional Listeners to Gateway API

The per-listener `type` field enables zero-downtime migration. Traditional NodePort/LoadBalancer listeners and TLSRoute listeners coexist on different ports.

### Step 1: Deploy the Gateway

Create the Gateway resource in your cluster:

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: redpanda-gateway
spec:
  gatewayClassName: envoy
  listeners:
    - name: kafka
      protocol: TLS
      port: 9094
      tls:
        mode: Passthrough
```

### Step 2: Add a TLSRoute listener alongside the existing one

Update your Helm values to add a new listener with `type: tlsroute`. The existing NodePort listener continues to work:

```yaml
external:
  enabled: true
  type: NodePort              # existing NodePort config unchanged
  gateway:
    enabled: true
    parentRefs:
      - name: redpanda-gateway
        sectionName: kafka
    advertisedPort: 9094
tls:
  enabled: true
  certs:
    default:
      caEnabled: true
listeners:
  kafka:
    external:
      default:                 # existing NodePort listener — unchanged
        port: 9094
        advertisedPorts:
          - 30092
      gw-listener:             # new TLSRoute listener on a different port
        port: 9095
        type: tlsroute
        host: redpanda.example.com
        hostTemplate: redpanda-$POD_ORDINAL-broker.example.com
        tls:
          cert: default
```

After `helm upgrade`, the cluster has both:
- **NodePort service** with port 9094 (for existing clients)
- **Gateway ClusterIP services + TLSRoutes** with port 9095 (for new clients)

The TLSRoutes are rendered **only for the `gw-listener` listener** — the NodePort `default` listener produces no routes. Because the route names embed the listener name (`gw-listener`) and the backend port is that listener's port (`9095`), they never collide with the traditional path:

```yaml
# Bootstrap for the gw-listener (host: redpanda.example.com, backend port 9095)
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: TLSRoute
metadata:
  name: redpanda-kafka-gw-listener-bootstrap
  namespace: default
spec:
  hostnames:
  - redpanda.example.com
  parentRefs:
  - name: kafka-gateway
    sectionName: kafka
  rules:
  - backendRefs:
    - name: redpanda-gateway-bootstrap
      port: 9095
---
# Per-broker (one per replica; $POD_ORDINAL → 0 shown)
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: TLSRoute
metadata:
  name: redpanda-kafka-gw-listener-0
  namespace: default
spec:
  hostnames:
  - redpanda-0-broker.example.com
  parentRefs:
  - name: kafka-gateway
    sectionName: kafka
  rules:
  - backendRefs:
    - name: gw-redpanda-0
      port: 9095
---
# redpanda-kafka-gw-listener-1 → redpanda-1-broker.example.com → gw-redpanda-1:9095
# redpanda-kafka-gw-listener-2 → redpanda-2-broker.example.com → gw-redpanda-2:9095
```

> Note `advertisedPort: 443` in the values above is what brokers advertise in metadata; the TLSRoute `backendRefs.port` is still the listener's own `9095`. These are independent on purpose.

### Step 3: Configure DNS and migrate clients

1. Set up DNS records pointing to the Gateway IP
2. Migrate clients one at a time to the new bootstrap address (`redpanda.example.com:9094`)
3. Monitor that clients are connecting through the Gateway

### Step 4: Remove the old listener

Once all clients have migrated, remove the NodePort listener:

```yaml
listeners:
  kafka:
    external:
      # default: removed
      gw-listener:
        port: 9095
        type: tlsroute
        host: redpanda.example.com
        hostTemplate: redpanda-$POD_ORDINAL-broker.example.com
        tls:
          cert: default
```

Optionally remove `external.type: NodePort` as it is no longer used.

## Verified end-to-end with Envoy Gateway + `rpk`

Reproducible recipe used to validate this PR on a local k3d cluster, producing and consuming over TLS through the Gateway. Run from the `feat/gateway-api-tlsroute` branch.

### 1. Cluster + dependencies

```bash
# Cluster (any K8s 1.30+ should work)
k3d cluster create rp-gw-test --image rancher/k3s:v1.32.13-k3s1

# Gateway API CRDs — TLSRoute is in the experimental channel, you must use experimental-install.yaml
kubectl apply -f https://github.com/kubernetes-sigs/gateway-api/releases/download/v1.2.1/experimental-install.yaml

# Envoy Gateway (any TLSRoute-capable Gateway implementation works; Cilium / Istio also fine)
helm install eg oci://docker.io/envoyproxy/gateway-helm \
  --version v1.2.6 \
  --namespace envoy-gateway-system --create-namespace \
  --wait

# Envoy Gateway does not auto-create a default GatewayClass; create one
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: eg
spec:
  controllerName: gateway.envoyproxy.io/gatewayclass-controller
EOF

# cert-manager (for the chart's self-signed CA)
helm install cert-manager jetstack/cert-manager \
  --namespace cert-manager --create-namespace \
  --version v1.17.2 --set crds.enabled=true --wait
```

### 2. Create a Gateway (user-managed, the chart only attaches TLSRoutes)

```bash
kubectl create namespace rp-gw
kubectl apply -f - <<EOF
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: Gateway
metadata:
  name: redpanda-gateway
  namespace: rp-gw
spec:
  gatewayClassName: eg
  listeners:
    - name: kafka
      protocol: TLS
      port: 9094
      tls:
        mode: Passthrough
      allowedRoutes:
        kinds:
          - kind: TLSRoute
            group: gateway.networking.k8s.io
EOF
```

### 3. Install the Redpanda chart with a gateway-mode listener

`values.yaml`:

```yaml
statefulset:
  replicas: 1
storage:
  persistentVolume:
    enabled: false
external:
  enabled: true
  domain: test.local                       # appended to the cert SANs as *.test.local
  gateway:
    enabled: true
    parentRefs:
      - name: redpanda-gateway
        sectionName: kafka
    advertisedPort: 9094                   # port advertised in broker metadata
tls:
  enabled: true
  certs:
    default:
      caEnabled: true
listeners:
  kafka:
    external:
      default:
        port: 9094
        type: tlsroute                      # opt this listener into TLSRoute mode
        host: redpanda.test.local          # bootstrap SNI hostname
        hostTemplate: redpanda-$POD_ORDINAL.test.local   # per-broker SNI hostname
        tls:
          enabled: true
          cert: default
```

```bash
helm install rp ./charts/redpanda/chart -n rp-gw -f values.yaml --wait
```

What the chart renders:

| Resource | Name | Notes |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `TLSRoute` | `rp-kafka-default-bootstrap` | hostname `redpanda.test.local` → `Service/rp-gateway-bootstrap:9094` |
| `TLSRoute` | `rp-kafka-default-0` | hostname `redpanda-0.test.local` → `Service/gw-rp-0:9094` |
| `Service` (ClusterIP) | `rp-gateway-bootstrap` | LB to all brokers on port 9094 |
| `Service` (ClusterIP) | `gw-rp-0` | per-broker, selects pod `rp-0` |
| `Certificate` | `rp-default-cert` | SANs include `*.test.local` and `test.local`, covering both hostnames |

Verify the routes are attached:

```bash
$ kubectl -n rp-gw get tlsroute
NAME                         AGE
rp-kafka-default-0           1m
rp-kafka-default-bootstrap   1m

$ kubectl -n rp-gw get gateway redpanda-gateway -o jsonpath='{.status.listeners[*].attachedRoutes}'
2

$ kubectl -n rp-gw get tlsroute -o jsonpath='{.items[*].status.parents[*].conditions[?(@.type=="Accepted")].status}'
True True
```

### 4. Connect with `rpk` over TLS

For local testing without DNS, run `rpk` in a container on the same docker network as the cluster, mapping the SNI hostnames to the Envoy data-plane IP via `--add-host`:

```bash
# Extract the chart-issued CA
kubectl -n rp-gw get secret rp-default-root-certificate -o jsonpath='{.data.ca\.crt}' | base64 -d > ca.crt

# Find the Envoy data-plane LoadBalancer IP
GW_IP=$(kubectl -n envoy-gateway-system get svc \
  -l gateway.envoyproxy.io/owning-gateway-name=redpanda-gateway \
  -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.loadBalancer.ingress[0].ip}')

# Wrapper that runs rpk inside the docker network, with hostname resolution + CA mounted
RPK="docker run --rm -i --network k3d-rp-gw-test \
  --add-host redpanda.test.local:$GW_IP \
  --add-host redpanda-0.test.local:$GW_IP \
  -v $PWD/ca.crt:/etc/rp/ca.crt:ro \
  --entrypoint rpk docker.redpanda.com/redpandadata/redpanda:v25.2.5 \
  -X brokers=redpanda.test.local:9094 \
  -X tls.enabled=true -X tls.ca=/etc/rp/ca.crt"

$RPK cluster info
$RPK topic create gateway-test -p 3 -r 1
printf 'key-1\thello' | $RPK topic produce gateway-test --format '%k\t%v'
$RPK topic consume gateway-test -n 1 -o :end -f '%p:%o key=%k value=%v\n'
```

Result on the validation run:

```
$ rpk cluster info
ID    HOST                   PORT
0*    redpanda-0.test.local  9094

$ rpk topic create gateway-test -p 3 -r 1

$ rpk topic produce gateway-test            # 5 records, partitions 0 + 2
Produced to partition 0 at offset 0 …
Produced to partition 2 at offset 0 …
…

$ rpk topic consume gateway-test -n 5 -o :end
```

SNI-based routing confirmed in the Envoy data-plane access log:

| `requested_server_name` | `upstream_cluster` |
| --- | --- |
| `redpanda.test.local` | `tlsroute/rp-gw/rp-kafka-default-bootstrap/rule/-1` |
| `redpanda-0.test.local` | `tlsroute/rp-gw/rp-kafka-default-0/rule/-1` |

So the design works end-to-end: bootstrap connection → bootstrap TLSRoute → bootstrap service; then the broker advertises `redpanda-0.test.local:9094`; the client SNI-reconnects; Envoy routes by SNI to the per-broker TLSRoute → per-broker ClusterIP → broker pod, all under TLS Passthrough using Redpanda's own cert (no Gateway-side cert needed).

## Files changed

| File | Change |
|------|--------|
| `charts/redpanda/values.go` | `GatewayConfig`, `GatewayParentRef` types; per-listener `Gateway`/`Host`/`HostTemplate` fields; `ServicePorts()` filters gateway listeners |
| `charts/redpanda/service.gateway.go` | Bootstrap + per-broker ClusterIP service generation (gateway-opted listeners only) |
| `charts/redpanda/tlsroute.go` | Bootstrap + per-broker TLSRoute generation with SNI hostnames |
| `charts/redpanda/chart.go` | Register TLSRoute type and wire into render pipeline |
| `charts/redpanda/secrets.go` | Per-listener gateway-aware advertised address construction |
| `charts/redpanda/service.{loadbalancer,nodeport}.go` | Skip gateway-opted listeners in port generation |

| `charts/redpanda/render_state_nogotohelm.go` | Operator render path converts the lightweight `*TLSRoute` to the upstream `gatewayv1alpha2.TLSRoute` so the syncer's `Types()` invariant holds (fixes gateway reconcile) |
| `operator/internal/telemetry/{collector,payload}.go` | `gatewayAPIExternalAccessEnabled` adoption counter |

## Telemetry

Adoption of Gateway API external access is reported through the operator's anonymous telemetry. `payload.redpanda.gatewayAPIExternalAccessEnabled` counts `Redpanda` clusters with `spec.external.gateway.enabled`, alongside the existing per-cluster feature counters (TLS, SASL, tiered storage, console). Implemented in `operator/internal/telemetry` (`collector.go` + `payload.go`); a unit test asserts the counter is 1 for a gateway-enabled cluster and 0 otherwise.

## External edge load balancer (Envoy Gateway) — AWS / GCP / Azure

This chart renders only TLSRoutes + per-broker **ClusterIP** services; it never creates a cloud load balancer. The single edge load balancer that fronts the whole cluster is provisioned by your Gateway implementation's data-plane Service. With **Envoy Gateway** you control its type and cloud annotations via an `EnvoyProxy` resource referenced from the `GatewayClass` `parametersRef`. One load balancer fronts *all* brokers — per-broker addressing is done by SNI, not by per-broker LBs (this is what resolves the "one LB per broker" problem).

Base wiring (identical on every cloud — only the `annotations`/`type` differ):

```yaml
apiVersion: gateway.envoyproxy.io/v1alpha1
kind: EnvoyProxy
metadata:
  name: rp-lb
  namespace: envoy-gateway-system
spec:
  provider:
    type: Kubernetes
    kubernetes:
      envoyService:
        type: LoadBalancer
        annotations: {}          # cloud-specific — see below
---
apiVersion: gateway.networking.k8s.io/v1
kind: GatewayClass
metadata:
  name: eg
spec:
  controllerName: gateway.envoyproxy.io/gatewayclass-controller
  parametersRef:                 # <- attaches the EnvoyProxy above
    group: gateway.envoyproxy.io
    kind: EnvoyProxy
    name: rp-lb
    namespace: envoy-gateway-system
```

> The `EnvoyProxy` must exist and be referenced by the `GatewayClass` **before** the data-plane Service is created. If you change it later, delete the Envoy service (`kubectl -n envoy-gateway-system delete svc -l gateway.envoyproxy.io/owning-gateway-name=<gw>`) so Envoy Gateway recreates it with the new annotations — cloud providers do not convert an existing LB's type in place.

### AWS — Network Load Balancer (NLB)

Two supported ways:

**a) In-tree cloud provider (no extra controller).** Validated on EKS 1.36.

```yaml
      envoyService:
        type: LoadBalancer
        annotations:
          service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: nlb
          service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
          # See the cross-zone note below:
          service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-cross-zone-load-balancing-enabled: "true"
```

**b) AWS Load Balancer Controller (recommended for production)** — IP-target NLB:

```yaml
      envoyService:
        type: LoadBalancer
        annotations:
          service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-type: external
          service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-nlb-target-type: ip
          service.beta.kubernetes.io/aws-load-balancer-scheme: internet-facing
```

> **Cross-zone gotcha (important for multi-AZ Kafka).** Envoy Gateway's data-plane Service uses `externalTrafficPolicy: Local`, so only nodes running an Envoy replica pass the NLB health check. NLB **cross-zone load balancing is OFF by default**, so an NLB IP in an AZ with no Envoy replica blackholes traffic. Either enable cross-zone (annotation above, or `aws elbv2 modify-load-balancer-attributes --attributes Key=load_balancing.cross_zone.enabled,Value=true`) **or** run ≥1 Envoy replica per AZ (`EnvoyProxy.spec.provider.kubernetes.envoyDeployment.replicas`). `target-type: ip` (option b) sidesteps this by targeting pods directly.

### GCP — passthrough Network Load Balancer (GKE)

A default `type: LoadBalancer` on GKE is already an **external passthrough Network LB** (L4), which is what TLS passthrough needs — no annotation required. For the newer backend-service-based NLB (recommended), set it **at creation**:

```yaml
      envoyService:
        type: LoadBalancer
        annotations:
          cloud.google.com/l4-rbs: "enabled"     # backend-service-based external passthrough NLB
```

GKE ≥ 1.33.1 alternative (preferred — always backend-service-based): set `spec.loadBalancerClass: networking.gke.io/l4-regional-external` on the Service. Internal instead of external: `networking.gke.io/load-balancer-type: "Internal"`.

### Azure — Standard Load Balancer (AKS)

A default `type: LoadBalancer` on AKS is a **public Standard Load Balancer** (L4), suitable for TLS passthrough — no annotation required. Internal only:

```yaml
      envoyService:
        type: LoadBalancer
        annotations:
          service.beta.kubernetes.io/azure-load-balancer-internal: "true"
```

### Apply (any cloud)

```bash
kubectl apply -f envoyproxy.yaml                 # EnvoyProxy + GatewayClass(parametersRef)
# if the Gateway/Service already existed with a different LB type:
kubectl -n envoy-gateway-system delete svc -l gateway.envoyproxy.io/owning-gateway-name=redpanda-gateway
kubectl -n envoy-gateway-system get svc -l gateway.envoyproxy.io/owning-gateway-name=redpanda-gateway -w   # wait for EXTERNAL-IP
```

### Validated on EKS 1.36 (operator path)

Built the operator from this branch (`linux/amd64`, pushed to ECR), deployed it with a `Redpanda` CR (3 brokers, `external.gateway` mode) on **EKS 1.36** + Envoy Gateway v1.8.1. Confirmed end-to-end:

- **One edge load balancer fronts all 3 brokers** (per-broker addressing via SNI, not per-broker LBs) — first a default Classic ELB, then re-provisioned as a **real NLB** (`type: network`, internet-facing, cross-zone enabled). This is the consolidation requested in redpanda-data/helm-charts#574.
- **Per-broker SNI cert coverage**: the managed broker cert's SANs include `redpanda.example.com` + `redpanda-{0,1,2}.example.com` (hosts with no covering wildcard), so TLS hostname verification succeeds on per-broker reconnect.
- **Fail-closed**: the CRD rejects `gateway.enabled` with empty `parentRefs` at admission (`minItems: 1`); the kafka gateway listener is excluded from the NodePort Service.
- **OMB 1 Mbps, produce *and* consume, 5-min steady state, zero errors / zero backlog:**
  - via in-cluster ClusterIP: avg 4.1 ms · p50 4.0 · p99 9.8 · p99.99 16.9 ms
  - via the NLB: avg 6.0 ms · p50 6.0 · p99 13.2 · p99.99 24.7 ms (the delta is the NLB hairpin)

## Out of scope (future work)

- TCPRoute support (for non-TLS listeners)
- Gateway resource management by the operator
- East-west (service mesh) traffic routing
- TLSRoute status checking (wait for gateway acceptance)

## Test plan

- [x] Verify chart compiles: `go build ./charts/redpanda/...`
- [x] Verify operator compiles: `go build ./operator/...`
- [x] Golden test: `gateway-api-tlsroute` — all listeners on TLSRoute
- [x] Golden test: `gateway-api-migration` — NodePort + TLSRoute coexisting
- [x] Full `TestTemplate` suite passes with no regressions
- [x] Manual testing with Envoy Gateway — full produce/consume via `rpk` over TLS, SNI routing verified (recipe + results above)
- [ ] Regenerate templates via `task generate` in CI

Closes #1361
Closes redpanda-data/helm-charts#574 (single edge load balancer fronting all brokers via SNI — see [External edge load balancer](#external-edge-load-balancer-envoy-gateway--aws--gcp--azure))

The external-access opt-in is modeled as a per-listener `type: tlsroute` (an alias layer over the cluster-wide `external.type`) instead of a `gateway: true` boolean — see [External access model](#external-access-model-per-listener-type-alias-layer). No `gateway: true` flag is carried; `type` is the single, forward-compatible opt-in.
